tours.name: The Lodes
tours.blurb: Down the South Fork from Mullan to Kellogg — the silver-lead lodes that made this narrow valley the richest mining ground in Idaho.

keys.cap: Mullan, under the Morning and the Gold Hunter, located 1884–85 — the upper end of a ten-mile string of lead. The Schitsu'umsh, the Coeur d'Alene people whose name the district borrowed, knew this country for millennia before any location notice; by the time Ransome came to map, the 1889 cession had pushed their reservation far southwest of their own mountains.

Wallace, seat of the district, at the meeting of every canyon — Placer, Ninemile, Canyon Creek. Founded 1884 as Placer Center; by 1908 two transcontinental railroads fought for room along this one street of river.

Up Big Creek, the Sunshine — located as a quartz claim in 1884 and worked patiently for decades before it proved the richest silver mine in America: over 360 million ounces, and in 1972 the fire in its depths that killed ninety-one men.

Kellogg and Wardner: the Bunker Hill and Sullivan, located in September 1885 — legend gives the discovery to Noah Kellogg's wandering jackass — for the better part of a century the greatest lead mine in America.

tours.name: Burke Canyon
tours.blurb: Seven miles of canyon so narrow the railroad ran through the hotel — Tiger, Poorman, Standard, Hecla, and the Hercules.

keys.cap: Into Canyon Creek at Gem — mills, tramways and boarding houses shoulder to shoulder up a gorge with no flat ground to spare. Ransome's plate inks a mine symbol at every bend.

Burke, at the head of the canyon, where the walls close to three hundred feet: the Tiger Hotel of 1896 was built clear across creek, road and track together — the trains ran straight through the hotel.

The Tiger and the Poorman, located 1884 on opposite walls, sued each other for years and then married in 1888 — among the first mines anywhere run on electric power, a thousand feet down under the creek.

The Hercules — a share-and-share grubstake of Burke cooks, trainmen and a boarding-house keeper named May Arkwright Hutton. Sixteen years of Sunday digging; in June 1901 the lead came in, and May spent her fortune winning women the vote.

tours.name: The Labor Wars
tours.blurb: 1892 and 1899, plainly: dynamite at the Frisco mill and the Bunker Hill concentrator, martial law twice, a thousand men in the bullpen.

keys.cap: July 11, 1892: the union struck against a wage cut, the companies filled the canyon with Pinkerton spies and armed guards, and after a dawn gun battle at Gem the miners sent giant powder down the Frisco mill's penstock and blew it off its foundations. Six men died; martial law followed.

April 29, 1899: a thousand masked miners seized a Northern Pacific train at Burke — the Dynamite Express — rode it the length of the district, and levelled the Bunker Hill concentrator at Wardner, the biggest in the world, with three thousand pounds of powder.

Governor Steunenberg asked McKinley for the Army. Black regulars of the 24th Infantry, home from Cuba, swept roughly a thousand men into a barn-and-boxcar prison at Kellogg — the bullpen — without warrants; some sat into the fall, and no one was convicted of the blast.

The owners' permit system — no job without papers renouncing the union — broke the Western Federation of Miners in the district. In 1905 Steunenberg died by a bomb at his own gate, and the 1907 Haywood trial put the Coeur d'Alene on every front page in America.

tours.blurb: August 20, 1910: the Big Burn takes the east third of Wallace, and Ed Pulaski holds forty-five men in a mine tunnel above town.

keys.cap: August 20, 1910. After the driest summer anyone could remember, a hurricane wind gathered a thousand small fires into one. That night it came over the ridge into Wallace and took the east third of the town; the last train out left under falling cinders.
Up Placer Creek, ranger Ed Pulaski was gathering his scattered crews when the blowup cut the trail back to town. He knew one way out: an old prospect adit on the West Fork.

Forty-five men and two horses lay in the dark of the Nicholson adit while the mouth timbers burned; Pulaski held the doorway with a pistol — the next man who tried to run would be shot. Five died. Forty walked out at dawn, and the peak above carries his name.

In two days the Big Burn crossed three million acres of Idaho and Montana and killed 78 firefighters. It hardened the young Forest Service's whole doctrine of suppression — and the hand tool in every fire cache since carries Pulaski's name.
